assessments.prompt: Explain to someone how you decide whether a counting problem needs permutations or combinations, walking through one worked example of each.
assessments.modelAnswer: The entire decision comes down to one question: if you swapped the order or roles of the items you selected, would you end up with a genuinely different outcome for the problem at hand? If swapping order matters, you need permutations; if it doesn't, you need combinations. Take assigning gold, silver, and bronze medals to 3 of 10 race finalists as the permutation example: giving Alice gold and Bob silver is a completely different result from giving Bob gold and Alice silver, even though the same two people were involved either way, because which specific medal each person receives matters. The count is 10P3 = 10!/7! = 720, using the multiplication principle's logic of 10 choices for gold, 9 remaining choices for silver, 8 remaining choices for bronze. Now take selecting which 3 of those same 10 finalists get invited to a bonus round, where being invited is all that matters and there's no ranking among the 3 invitees: inviting {Alice, Bob, Carol} is exactly the same outcome no matter what order you happened to write those three names down in, so order doesn't matter here, and you need combinations instead: 10C3 = 10!/(3!7!) = 120. Notice 720 is exactly 6 times larger than 120, and 6 = 3! -- that's not a coincidence, it's because each of the 120 unordered groups of 3 corresponds to exactly 3! = 6 different possible medal orderings, which is exactly why the combination formula divides the permutation formula by r! in general: it's systematically collapsing every group of r! duplicate orderings down into the single group they all represent.

concepts.title: Conditional Probability and the Multiplication Rule
concepts.description: Conditional probability formalizes what happens to your beliefs once you learn some event already occurred -- it shrinks the sample space down to just that event -- and the multiplication rule that falls out of its definition is what lets you compute joint probabilities of sequences of dependent events, while confusing P(A given B) with P(B given A), the prosecutor's fallacy, is one of the most consequential and recurring errors in both statistics and applied ML evaluation.
learningObjectives: Define P(A given B) = P(A intersect B) / P(B) and explain the sample-space-shrinking intuition behind it.
Apply the multiplication (chain) rule to compute the joint probability of several dependent events occurring in sequence.
Define independence formally via P(A given B) = P(A), equivalently P(A intersect B) = P(A) x P(B), and distinguish it precisely from mutual exclusivity.
Identify the prosecutor's fallacy -- confusing P(A given B) with P(B given A) -- in a concrete numeric example and explain why the two quantities can differ enormously.
Compute conditional probabilities from a joint frequency table in code, and connect conditional probability to class-conditional likelihoods used by ML classifiers.

sections.heading: Conditional Probability: Shrinking the Sample Space
sections.body:
**Conditional probability**, P(A | B) (read "the probability of A given B"), asks: once you already know event B happened, what's the probability that A also happened? It's formally defined as **P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)**, valid whenever P(B) > 0. The intuition behind this ratio is a direct extension of the classical-probability idea from the first concept in this module: learning that B occurred effectively shrinks your entire universe of possibilities from Omega down to just B -- outcomes outside B are no longer live possibilities at all -- and P(A | B) asks what fraction of that *new, smaller* universe also satisfies A. In an equally-likely-outcomes space, this is exactly |A ∩ B| / |B|, the same counting logic as before, just restricted to the smaller space B instead of the full Omega.

Take a single die roll: let A = "the roll is 4" and B = "the roll is even" = {2, 4, 6}. Once you know B happened, the only remaining possibilities are {2, 4, 6} -- three equally likely outcomes, not six -- and exactly one of those three, namely 4, also satisfies A. So P(A | B) = 1/3, not the unconditional P(A) = 1/6. Conditioning genuinely changed the probability, because knowing the roll was even makes a 4 more likely than it was before you had that information (you've ruled out three odd numbers that could never have been the answer anyway).

```python
omega = set(range(1, 7))
A = {4}
B = {2, 4, 6}

# Direct definition: P(A | B) = P(A intersect B) / P(B)
p_A_given_B = len(A & B) / len(omega) / (len(B) / len(omega))
print(p_A_given_B)   # 0.333...

# Equivalent shortcut for equally-likely spaces: restrict to B, then count A within it
p_A_given_B_shortcut = len(A & B) / len(B)
print(p_A_given_B_shortcut)   # 0.333..., matches exactly
```

sections.heading: The Multiplication (Chain) Rule for Joint Probabilities
sections.body:
Rearranging the definition of conditional probability gives the **multiplication rule**: **P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B) x P(B)**, equivalently P(A ∩ B) = P(B | A) x P(A). This is the tool for computing the probability that *several* events all happen together, in sequence, especially when later events depend on earlier ones. Drawing two cards from a deck *without* replacement is the classic example: the probability of drawing an ace first, then a second ace, is **P(ace1) x P(ace2 | ace1)** = (4/52) x (3/51) -- the second term is smaller than 4/52 precisely because one ace and one card overall have already been removed from the deck by the time the second draw happens, so the two draws are not independent.

This extends to any number of sequential events via the **chain rule**: P(A1 ∩ A2 ∩ ... ∩ An) = P(A1) x P(A2 | A1) x P(A3 | A1 ∩ A2) x ... x P(An | A1 ∩ ... ∩ An-1) -- each term conditions on everything that came before it. Note this decomposition is always exactly true, by repeated application of the multiplication rule, regardless of whether the events are independent; independence is what would let you *simplify* each conditional term back down to an unconditional one, which is exactly the next section's subject.

```python
import math

# P(draw 2 aces in a row, without replacement) via the chain rule
p_ace1 = 4 / 52
p_ace2_given_ace1 = 3 / 51        # one ace and one card already removed
p_both_aces_chain_rule = p_ace1 * p_ace2_given_ace1

# Cross-check via combinations from the previous concept
p_both_aces_via_counting = math.comb(4, 2) / math.comb(52, 2)

print(p_both_aces_chain_rule, p_both_aces_via_counting)   # both ~0.00452
```

For machine learning engineers, the chain rule is not just a card-counting trick -- it is the exact mathematical structure underneath **autoregressive sequence models**, including modern language models. The probability of an entire token sequence x1, x2, ..., xn is decomposed as P(x1) x P(x2 | x1) x P(x3 | x1, x2) x ... x P(xn | x1, ..., xn-1), and a language model is, mechanically, a function that estimates each of those conditional next-token probabilities -- generating text one token at a time by repeatedly sampling from P(next token | everything so far) is the chain rule, applied live.

sections.heading: Independence, Formally Defined
sections.body:
Two events A and B are formally **independent** when knowing B occurred doesn't change the probability of A at all: **P(A | B) = P(A)**. Substituting this into the multiplication rule, P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B) x P(B) = P(A) x P(B), gives the algebraically equivalent, and more commonly quoted, definition: **P(A ∩ B) = P(A) x P(B)**. A short algebraic check shows independence is symmetric -- if P(A | B) = P(A), then P(B | A) = P(A ∩ B)/P(A) = [P(A) x P(B)] / P(A) = P(B), meaning B is independent of A exactly whenever A is independent of B, in either direction.

This is the moment to fully resolve the mutual-exclusivity-versus-independence distinction first raised in the previous concept, now with the formal tool in hand. If A and B are mutually exclusive (A ∩ B = ∅) and both have nonzero probability, then P(A ∩ B) = 0, but independence would require P(A ∩ B) = P(A) x P(B) > 0 -- a contradiction, so genuinely possible mutually exclusive events are never independent. But the reverse relationship, independent-and-not-mutually-exclusive, is completely ordinary: flip a fair coin twice, and let A = "first flip is heads," B = "second flip is heads." These events plainly *can* co-occur (both heads is a real outcome), so they aren't mutually exclusive, yet P(A ∩ B) = 1/4 = (1/2) x (1/2) = P(A) x P(B), so they are independent. Mutual exclusivity and independence sit on two genuinely different axes, and the four combinations -- mutually exclusive or not, crossed with independent or not -- are not all equally populated: mutually-exclusive-and-independent is impossible for nontrivial events, but every other combination is possible.

```python
import itertools

omega = set(itertools.product(["H", "T"], repeat=2))
A = {o for o in omega if o[0] == "H"}     # first flip heads
B = {o for o in omega if o[1] == "H"}     # second flip heads

p_A, p_B = len(A) / len(omega), len(B) / len(omega)
p_A_and_B = len(A & B) / len(omega)

print(p_A_and_B, p_A * p_B)         # 0.25 0.25 -- independent
print(A & B)                          # {('H','H')} -- not mutually exclusive; they DO co-occur
```

sections.heading: P(A | B) is Not P(B | A): The Prosecutor's Fallacy
sections.body:
The **prosecutor's fallacy** is the error of treating P(A | B) and P(B | A) as if they were the same number, or close to it, when in general they can differ enormously. The name comes from courtroom reasoning: a prosecutor argues "the probability of this DNA match occurring by pure chance, given the defendant is innocent, is only 1 in a million -- therefore the probability the defendant is innocent, given the DNA match, is only 1 in a million." The first quantity, P(match | innocent), might genuinely be tiny, but the second quantity, P(innocent | match), is a completely different number that also depends heavily on how many people *could* have been tested and how rare true guilt is in the first place -- silently swapping which side of the conditioning bar each fact belongs on turns a specific, narrow technical claim into a wildly different, much stronger-sounding claim about the very thing actually in question.

A concrete numeric version makes the gap unmistakable. Suppose a rare condition affects 1 in 10,000 people, and a diagnostic test correctly flags 99% of true cases (so P(positive | has condition) = 0.99) while also, unavoidably, flagging 1% of healthy people as false positives (P(positive | no condition) = 0.01). It's extremely tempting to read "99% accurate test, tested positive" as "99% likely to actually have the condition" -- but that conflates P(positive | condition) with the very different quantity actually being asked for, P(condition | positive). Fully resolving this gap requires combining the multiplication rule with the law of total probability, which is exactly the subject of the next two concepts in this module -- for now, the essential habit to build is simply recognizing, on sight, which direction a stated conditional probability runs, and refusing to silently flip it.

This exact error transplants directly into everyday ML evaluation. A classifier's **recall** (or sensitivity) is P(predicted positive | actually positive), while its **precision** is P(actually positive | predicted positive) -- these are literally P(B | A) and P(A | B) for the same pair of events, and they can differ dramatically, especially when positives are rare in the underlying population (exactly the situation the medical test example sets up). Reporting a model's recall while letting a stakeholder assume it describes precision -- or vice versa -- is the prosecutor's fallacy wearing a different name, and it is one of the single most common miscommunications between ML engineers and the business stakeholders consuming their model's metrics.

examples.title: P(A|B) vs P(B|A) From a Joint Frequency Table
examples.code:
import numpy as np

# Rows: has_condition (yes/no); Columns: test_result (positive/negative)
# Counts out of a population of 10,000
#                 positive   negative
# has_condition:      95         5
# no_condition:      495      9405

table = np.array([
    [95,    5],
    [495, 9405],
])

p_positive_given_condition = table[0, 0] / table[0, :].sum()
p_condition_given_positive = table[0, 0] / table[:, 0].sum()

print(round(p_positive_given_condition, 4))   # 0.95 -- the test's sensitivity
print(round(p_condition_given_positive, 4))   # 0.1610 -- very different!
examples.explanation: Building an explicit joint frequency table and computing both conditional probabilities from it -- dividing along a row for P(positive | condition), versus dividing down a column for P(condition | positive) -- makes the prosecutor's fallacy impossible to fall into by accident, because the two divisions are visibly different operations on visibly different subsets of the same table. The dramatic gap between 0.95 and 0.161 here previews exactly why the next two concepts (the law of total probability and Bayes' theorem) exist: turning a known P(positive | condition) into the practically far more useful P(condition | positive) requires more than just reading the number off the table in the other direction -- it requires properly accounting for how rare the condition is in the whole population, which is precisely what Bayes' theorem, two concepts from now, formalizes.

examples.title: The Chain Rule for Sequential Draws Without Replacement
examples.code:
import math

def p_no_aces_in_n_draws(n, deck_size=52, aces=4):
    p = 1.0
    remaining_deck = deck_size
    remaining_non_aces = deck_size - aces
    for _ in range(n):
        p *= remaining_non_aces / remaining_deck
        remaining_deck -= 1
        remaining_non_aces -= 1
    return p

chain_rule_result = p_no_aces_in_n_draws(5)

# Cross-check via combinations: choose all 5 cards from the 48 non-aces
combinatorial_result = math.comb(48, 5) / math.comb(52, 5)

print(round(chain_rule_result, 6), round(combinatorial_result, 6))   # match exactly
examples.explanation: This example computes 'no aces in 5 draws without replacement' two structurally different ways and shows they agree exactly: the chain-rule version multiplies five successive conditional probabilities, each one accounting for exactly which cards have already been removed from the deck by that point, while the combinatorial version (reusing the previous concept's tools) counts the number of 5-card hands drawn entirely from the 48 non-ace cards, divided by the total number of 5-card hands. Getting identical answers from two independently-derived methods is a strong, general debugging technique for probability code -- whenever a sequential chain-rule calculation and a direct combinatorial count of the same event disagree, one of the two computations has a bug, and this cross-check finds it before the wrong number ever reaches a downstream decision.

examples.title: Checking Independence Empirically on a Small Feature Dataset
examples.code:
import numpy as np

# A tiny synthetic dataset: two binary features across 8 examples
has_feature_A = np.array([1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0])
has_feature_B = np.array([1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1])

p_A = has_feature_A.mean()
p_B = has_feature_B.mean()
p_A_and_B = (has_feature_A & has_feature_B).mean()

print("P(A):", p_A, "P(B):", p_B)
print("P(A and B):", p_A_and_B, "vs P(A)*P(B):", p_A * p_B)
print("Roughly independent?" , np.isclose(p_A_and_B, p_A * p_B, atol=0.1))
examples.explanation: Checking P(A intersect B) against P(A) x P(B) directly on real (here, synthetic) data is exactly the empirical procedure for testing whether an independence assumption is remotely defensible before relying on it -- and it's worth doing this check explicitly, because independence is very easy to assume by default and quietly wrong far more often than it's quietly right. This specific check is the empirical backbone of the conditional-independence assumption inside a Naive Bayes classifier (covered fully two concepts from now): a Naive Bayes model assumes each pair of features is conditionally independent given the class label, and running exactly this kind of comparison, separately within each class's subset of the data, is how you'd sanity-check whether that assumption is even approximately reasonable for a real dataset rather than accepting it purely on faith.

misconceptions.description: P(A given B) and P(B given A) are basically the same number, or at least always close to each other.
misconceptions.clarification: This is exactly the prosecutor's fallacy. The two quantities are generally different, and the gap between them can be enormous, especially when A and B have very different overall (unconditional) probabilities -- the joint frequency table example shows P(positive test | has condition) = 0.95 while P(has condition | positive test) = 0.161 for the very same population, an almost sixfold difference. The two are only guaranteed to be close when P(A) and P(B) happen to be close to each other, which is not something you can assume without checking; correctly converting one into the other in general requires the law of total probability and Bayes' theorem, covered in the next two concepts.

misconceptions.description: If two events can co-occur -- they are not mutually exclusive -- then they must be dependent on each other.
misconceptions.clarification: Mutual exclusivity and independence are separate properties, not opposites of each other. Two fair, separately-flipped coins give a clean counterexample: 'first flip heads' and 'second flip heads' can obviously co-occur (both heads is a real outcome, so they are not mutually exclusive), yet P(both heads) = 1/4 = P(first heads) x P(second heads), so they are independent as well. Being able to co-occur says nothing by itself about whether learning one event happened changes the probability of the other -- that's a separate question, answered only by actually comparing P(A given B) to P(A).

exercises.prompt: This code is supposed to compute the probability of drawing two aces in a row from a standard 52-card deck, without replacement, but it gives 0.00592 instead of the correct 0.00452. Find the bug and fix it.

exercises.solutionCode:

p_ace2_given_ace1 = 3 / 51   # fixed: one ace and one card already removed

p_both_aces = p_ace1 * p_ace2_given_ace1

exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code multiplies P(ace) by itself, which is only valid if the two draws were independent -- but drawing 'without replacement' means the first card drawn is gone from the deck by the time the second card is drawn, so the two events are explicitly dependent, and the multiplication rule requires the second term to be the true conditional probability P(ace on draw 2 | ace on draw 1) = 3/51 (3 aces remaining out of 51 remaining cards), not the unconditional 4/52 used for the first draw. Reusing 4/52 for both draws silently assumes independence that the 'without replacement' setup explicitly rules out, inflating the joint probability.

exercises.prompt: What do the two printed probabilities show, and what does the near-equality (or lack of it) between p_A_and_B and p_A * p_B tell you about events A and B?

    #  event_B_true  event_B_false

    [   45,               5],   # event_A_false

If p_A_and_B were equal to p_A * p_B, A and B would be independent; if they're meaningfully different, A and B are dependent -- knowing one changes the odds of the other.
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints 0.5 0.75 0.3, then 0.375. Since p_A_and_B (0.3) is noticeably less than p_A * p_B (0.375), events A and B are NOT independent -- knowing B is true actually makes A somewhat less likely than its baseline 0.5 (specifically, P(A|B) = 0.3/0.75 = 0.4, below the unconditional P(A) = 0.5), meaning A and B are dependent, with B's occurrence being mildly negative evidence against A.

assessments.prompt: Rolling one fair die, let A = 'the roll is 4' and B = 'the roll is even' = {2, 4, 6}. What is P(A | B), and why does it differ from the unconditional P(A) = 1/6?
options: P(A|B) = 1/6, identical to P(A), because conditioning on B never changes anything.
P(A|B) = 1/3, because once B is known to have occurred, the relevant sample space shrinks to just {2, 4, 6}, and exactly one of those three equally likely outcomes is a 4.
P(A|B) = 1/2, because A and B are the same event once you account for evenness.
P(A|B) cannot be computed, because 4 is one of the outcomes in B.
assessments.explanation: Conditioning on B restricts attention to the 3 equally likely outcomes {2, 4, 6}, of which exactly 1 (namely 4) also satisfies A, giving P(A|B) = 1/3 -- larger than the unconditional 1/6 because ruling out the three odd numbers makes a 4 relatively more likely among what remains. Option A is wrong because conditioning clearly can, and here does, change the probability. Option C confuses A and B, which are related but not identical (B contains 2 and 6 as well as 4). Option D is wrong -- P(A|B) is perfectly well-defined whenever P(B) > 0, and the fact that A's one outcome happens to lie inside B is exactly why P(A|B) is nonzero at all.

assessments.prompt: A stakeholder says: 'Our fraud model has 90% recall, meaning P(flagged as fraud | actually fraud) = 0.90 -- so a transaction the model flags as fraud has a 90% chance of actually being fraud.' What error is being made?
options: No error -- recall and this flagged-transaction probability are the same quantity.

The prosecutor's fallacy: recall is P(flagged | actually fraud), but 'chance a flagged transaction is really fraud' is the reversed conditional, P(actually fraud | flagged), which is a different quantity, especially when fraud is rare overall.
The error is that recall can never be as high as 90% for any real classifier.
The error is that fraud detection models cannot have a defined recall value.
assessments.explanation: Recall/sensitivity, P(flagged | actually fraud), and the flagged-transaction's actual fraud probability, P(actually fraud | flagged), are exactly the two directions of a conditional probability -- confusing them is precisely the prosecutor's fallacy described in the explanation, and the gap between them typically widens further the rarer fraud is in the overall transaction population (mirroring the medical-test example). Option A asserts the very confusion being tested as if it were correct. Option C and D are unrelated, fabricated claims -- nothing about this scenario limits how high recall can be or claims recall is undefined for fraud models.

assessments.prompt: Events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, and P(A intersect B) = 0.2. Are A and B independent, and how do you know?
options: Yes, independent, because P(A intersect B) = 0.2 is a positive number.
Yes, independent, because P(A) x P(B) = 0.4 x 0.5 = 0.2, which exactly equals the given P(A intersect B).
No, not independent, because P(A) and P(B) are different numbers.
Cannot be determined without also knowing whether A and B are mutually exclusive.
assessments.explanation: Independence is defined by the equality P(A intersect B) = P(A) x P(B); here P(A) x P(B) = 0.4 x 0.5 = 0.2, which matches the given P(A intersect B) = 0.2 exactly, so A and B are independent by definition. Option A is a non-sequitur -- a positive intersection probability alone says nothing about independence (it only rules out mutual exclusivity, a completely different property). Option C wrongly assumes independence requires equal individual probabilities, which the formal definition never requires. Option D is unnecessary -- independence is checked directly via the multiplication definition, and mutual exclusivity is a separate question this problem doesn't need answered at all.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a colleague what the chain rule is, work through one concrete example, and explain how this same rule underlies autoregressive language models.
assessments.modelAnswer: The chain rule falls directly out of rearranging the definition of conditional probability: since P(A given B) = P(A intersect B) / P(B), multiplying both sides by P(B) gives P(A intersect B) = P(A given B) x P(B), which says the probability of two events both happening equals the probability of the first happening, times the probability of the second happening given that the first already did. Extended to more than two events, this becomes P(A1 and A2 and ... and An) = P(A1) x P(A2 given A1) x P(A3 given A1 and A2) x ... x P(An given everything before it) -- each new term conditions on the full history of everything that came before it, and this decomposition is always exactly true, whether or not the events are actually dependent on each other. A concrete example: the probability of drawing two aces in a row from a deck, without replacement, is P(ace on draw 1) x P(ace on draw 2 given an ace was already drawn) = (4/52) x (3/51), and the second term is smaller than the first because one ace and one card overall have already left the deck by the time the second draw happens -- using 4/52 twice would incorrectly ignore that dependency. This exact structure -- decomposing a joint probability into a product of conditionals, each one built on everything before it -- is precisely how autoregressive language models are built: the probability of an entire generated sentence is the product, over every token in it, of that token's probability given every token that came before it, and the model itself is just a function trained to estimate each of those next-token conditional probabilities. Generating text one token at a time, feeding each new token back in as context for predicting the next one, is the chain rule being applied live, one factor at a time.

concepts.title: The Law of Total Probability
concepts.description: The law of total probability is the tool for computing the overall probability of an event by breaking the sample space into a partition of disjoint, exhaustive pieces and weighting each piece's conditional probability by how likely that piece is -- it is the exact mechanism that makes the denominator of Bayes' theorem, and marginalizing over any hidden or latent variable in an ML model, computable at all.
learningObjectives: Define a partition of a sample space and explain why its pieces must be both pairwise disjoint and collectively exhaustive.
Derive the law of total probability from the additivity axiom and the definition of conditional probability.
Apply the law of total probability to compute an overall probability by conditioning across a partition with more than two pieces.
Work a full multi-branch real-world example -- a medical test's overall positive rate across sub-populations with different prevalence -- from raw numbers through to a final answer.
Recognize when a probability computation implicitly requires marginalizing over a partition, such as a hidden class variable in a mixture model, and connect this to ML generative models.

sections.heading: Partitions: Slicing the Sample Space Into Disjoint, Exhaustive Pieces
sections.body:
A **partition** of the sample space Omega is a collection of events B1, B2, ..., Bn satisfying two conditions simultaneously: they are **pairwise disjoint** (Bi ∩ Bj = ∅ for every pair i ≠ j -- no outcome belongs to more than one piece) and **collectively exhaustive** (B1 ∪ B2 ∪ ... ∪ Bn = Omega -- every outcome belongs to at least one piece). Together, these two properties guarantee every single outcome in Omega belongs to *exactly one* Bi, with no double-counting and nothing left out. A population split into age brackets "under 30," "30 to 60," and "over 60" is a valid partition only if the brackets are drawn so that no one falls into two brackets at once and everyone in the population is captured by some bracket -- which sounds obvious stated this way, but real-world bucketing schemes get this wrong constantly (overlapping boundary definitions, or a "none of the above" group nobody remembered to include), and both failure modes silently break every calculation built on top of the partition.

It's worth being explicit about why *both* properties matter, because a scheme satisfying only one of them looks superficially fine while producing a genuinely wrong answer. If the pieces overlap (not disjoint), an outcome shared by two pieces gets its probability effectively counted twice when you sum across pieces. If the pieces don't cover everything (not exhaustive), some probability mass belongs to no piece at all, and any calculation that sums contributions "across all the pieces" silently omits it. Both failure modes are addressed directly by this concept's first misconception, because they are exactly the mistake beginners make when they assume "any reasonable-looking grouping" qualifies as a partition without actually checking.

sections.heading: Deriving the Law of Total Probability
sections.body:
Given a valid partition {B1, ..., Bn} of Omega, and any event A, the **law of total probability** states: **P(A) = Σᵢ P(A | Bi) x P(Bi)** -- the overall probability of A equals a weighted average of A's probability *within* each piece of the partition, weighted by how likely each piece is in the first place. The derivation is short and builds directly on tools from earlier in this module. Since {B1, ..., Bn} partitions Omega, the event A itself can be split into disjoint pieces: A = (A ∩ B1) ∪ (A ∩ B2) ∪ ... ∪ (A ∩ Bn) -- every outcome in A belongs to exactly one Bi, so it belongs to exactly one of these (A ∩ Bi) pieces. These pieces are pairwise disjoint (since the Bi are), so Kolmogorov's third axiom (additivity, from the earlier concept in this module) gives P(A) = Σᵢ P(A ∩ Bi). Finally, the multiplication rule from the previous concept rewrites each term as P(A ∩ Bi) = P(A | Bi) x P(Bi), giving exactly the formula above.

```python
import numpy as np

p_B = np.array([0.5, 0.3, 0.2])          # P(B_i) for each partition piece -- must sum to 1
p_A_given_B = np.array([0.10, 0.05, 0.40])  # P(A | B_i) within each piece

p_A = np.dot(p_A_given_B, p_B)             # exactly the law of total probability
print(p_A)                                  # 0.13
```

That single line, `np.dot(p_A_given_B, p_B)`, is the entire formula -- it isn't an approximation or a simplification, it is a literal weighted sum, and recognizing "I need to compute an overall probability by conditioning on some partition and weighting by how common each piece is" as exactly this dot-product pattern is the single most useful skill this concept builds.

sections.heading: Worked Example: A Medical Test Across Three Sub-Populations
sections.body:
Consider a screening test applied across a population made up of three age groups with genuinely different disease prevalence: **young** (40% of the population, 2% disease prevalence), **middle-aged** (35% of the population, 8% prevalence), and **older** (25% of the population, 20% prevalence). Suppose the test has the same 95% sensitivity in every group (P(positive | has disease) = 0.95 within each group) -- what is the overall probability that a randomly selected person from this population tests positive?

The three age groups form a valid partition (everyone falls into exactly one age group, by construction), so the law of total probability applies directly: P(positive) = P(positive | young) x P(young) + P(positive | middle) x P(middle) + P(positive | older) x P(older), where each P(positive | group) itself has to be computed first, since a person can test positive either by truly having the disease and testing positive (sensitivity) or by not having the disease and still testing positive (a false positive, requiring the test's false-positive rate, assumed here at 3% in every group).

```python
groups = ["young", "middle", "older"]
p_group = [0.40, 0.35, 0.25]
prevalence = [0.02, 0.08, 0.20]
sensitivity = 0.95
false_positive_rate = 0.03

p_positive_given_group = [
    sensitivity * prev + false_positive_rate * (1 - prev)
    for prev in prevalence
]

p_positive_overall = sum(pg * ppg for pg, ppg in zip(p_group, p_positive_given_group))

for g, ppg in zip(groups, p_positive_given_group):
    print(g, round(ppg, 4))
print("overall:", round(p_positive_overall, 4))
```

This overall figure -- a single blended positive rate -- is exactly a weighted average across sub-populations whose individual rates differ substantially (the older group's positive rate is noticeably higher than the young group's), and it directly illustrates a practical concern for anyone deploying a single model or a single threshold across a heterogeneous population: an aggregate metric can look perfectly reasonable while masking large differences between subgroups, which is precisely the kind of subgroup-level scrutiny that model fairness and distribution-shift audits are built to catch.

sections.heading: Marginalizing Over a Hidden Variable: Where This Shows Up in ML
sections.body:
The law of total probability generalizes far beyond splitting a human population into named sub-groups: any time there's a **hidden (latent) categorical variable** Z, and you want the probability of some *observable* outcome x without reference to which specific value of Z produced it, you compute exactly **P(x) = Σₖ P(x | Z=k) x P(Z=k)** -- summing, or "marginalizing," over every possible value the hidden variable could take. This is the exact mathematical operation a **Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM)** performs to compute the overall density of a data point: each of the K mixture components has its own probability P(Z=k) (the mixture weight) and its own conditional density P(x | Z=k) (a Gaussian centered at that component's mean), and the point's overall marginal density is the weighted sum across all K components -- structurally identical to the three-age-group medical test example, just with "which age group" replaced by "which mixture component."

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

# A 2-component 1-D Gaussian mixture
weights = [0.6, 0.4]                 # P(Z=0), P(Z=1) -- the hidden component
means = [0.0, 5.0]
stds = [1.0, 1.5]

x = 2.0
component_densities = [norm.pdf(x, loc=m, scale=s) for m, s in zip(means, stds)]
marginal_density = sum(w * d for w, d in zip(weights, component_densities))

print(component_densities)
print(marginal_density)   # the overall P(x) with the hidden component marginalized out
```

This "sum over a hidden category, weighted by that category's probability" pattern isn't a standalone curiosity -- it is precisely the computation that makes the denominator of **Bayes' theorem** tractable, which is the very next concept in this module. Bayes' theorem needs P(evidence), the total probability of observing some piece of evidence *regardless* of which underlying hypothesis is true, and that quantity is computed by summing the evidence's probability under each hypothesis, weighted by that hypothesis's prior probability -- which is exactly the law of total probability, applied to the partition formed by the competing hypotheses themselves.

examples.title: The Law of Total Probability as a Reusable Dot Product
examples.code:
import numpy as np

def total_probability(p_partition, p_A_given_partition):
    p_partition = np.asarray(p_partition)
    p_A_given_partition = np.asarray(p_A_given_partition)
    assert np.isclose(p_partition.sum(), 1.0), "partition probabilities must sum to 1"
    return float(np.dot(p_partition, p_A_given_partition))

# Example: 4-piece partition
p_B = [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25]
p_A_given_B = [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4]

print(total_probability(p_B, p_A_given_B))   # 0.25
examples.explanation: Wrapping the law of total probability in a small reusable function, with an explicit assertion that the partition probabilities sum to 1, turns an easy-to-forget validity requirement into a check that runs automatically every time the function is used -- exactly the kind of defensive habit worth building once a formula depends on an assumption (here, a genuine partition) that's easy to silently violate. Note that the function works for any number of partition pieces, not just two or three, precisely because the underlying formula is a general weighted sum, not a special-cased rule for small numbers of branches -- directly relevant to this concept's second misconception.

groups = ["young", "middle", "older"]
p_group = [0.40, 0.35, 0.25]
prevalence = [0.02, 0.08, 0.20]
sensitivity, fpr = 0.95, 0.03

p_positive_given_group = [sensitivity * prev + fpr * (1 - prev) for prev in prevalence]
p_positive_overall = sum(g * p for g, p in zip(p_group, p_positive_given_group))

for name, p in zip(groups, p_positive_given_group):
    print(f"{name}: P(positive | group) = {p:.4f}")
print(f"overall P(positive) = {p_positive_overall:.4f}")
examples.explanation: Running the numbers end to end shows the overall positive rate (roughly 8.5%) sits well above the young group's own rate (roughly 3.7%) and well below the older group's rate (roughly 20.9%) -- exactly the behavior expected of a weighted average, since the overall figure blends three genuinely different group-level rates according to how large each group is. This is worth internalizing precisely because a single reported number like 'our test's overall positive rate is 8.5%' can quietly hide the fact that it means something very different depending on which sub-population a given patient actually belongs to -- the same caution that applies to any single aggregate performance number reported for an ML model deployed across a demographically or behaviorally diverse user base.

examples.title: Marginal Density of a Gaussian Mixture Model
examples.explanation: marginal_density(x) is a direct, line-for-line translation of P(x) = sum_k P(x | Z=k) x P(Z=k): each term in the sum is one mixture component's density at x, scaled by that component's mixture weight, and adding them together marginalizes out the hidden component identity entirely, leaving only the probability of the observable value x. This function is, in miniature, exactly what a fitted GMM's score or predict_proba machinery computes internally for every point it's asked to evaluate -- seeing the formula written out explicitly here, rather than hidden behind a library call, is what makes the connection to the law of total probability concrete rather than something to take on faith.

misconceptions.description: As long as I sum P(A | B_i) weighted by P(B_i) over some collection of B_i's I've chosen, I get the correct P(A) -- any reasonable-looking grouping works.
misconceptions.clarification: The formula is only valid when the B_i genuinely form a partition -- pairwise disjoint AND collectively exhaustive. If the groups overlap, outcomes in the overlap get weighted and counted more than once, inflating the result; if the groups don't cover the whole sample space, some probability mass is left out entirely, deflating the result. For example, splitting a population into 'under 40' (50%) and 'over 30' (60%) is not a valid partition -- these overlap for ages 30-40, and the weights don't even sum to 1 (110%), which alone signals something is wrong before any conditional probabilities are even considered.

misconceptions.description: The law of total probability is really just a tool for two-branch (binary) situations, like a positive/negative medical test.
misconceptions.clarification: The formula generalizes to any finite (or even countably infinite) partition, with no limit on the number of pieces -- the derivation itself never assumes exactly two pieces, only that the B_i are disjoint and exhaustive. The worked medical-test example in this concept deliberately uses three sub-populations, and the mixture-model example generalizes further to however many components K a model happens to have, precisely to make clear that 'two branches' was never a structural requirement, just the simplest illustrative case.

exercises.prompt: This code computes an overall probability using the law of total probability, but the 'groups' used don't actually form a valid partition, and the resulting probability is nonsensical. Find the bug and explain what's wrong with the groups.

A sum greater than 1 across the group probabilities is a direct sign the groups overlap (some outcomes are being counted as part of more than one group), violating the 'pairwise disjoint' requirement.

The fix isn't just numerical (e.g. rescaling) -- the underlying groups themselves need to be redefined so they're genuinely disjoint and exhaustive before this formula can be trusted; here, redefining them as three truly non-overlapping groups summing to exactly 1.0 fixes it.

The law of total probability's derivation depends entirely on the groups forming a genuine partition of the sample space; feeding it overlapping (or non-exhaustive) groups doesn't raise an error, it just silently returns a number that isn't actually P(A). The fix is to redefine the groups so they are genuinely disjoint and exhaustive -- summing to exactly 1.0 -- and adding an explicit assertion catches this class of bug immediately rather than letting a wrong number flow downstream unnoticed.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following collections of events B1, B2, B3 qualifies as a valid partition of a sample space Omega?
options: Three events whose probabilities are 0.3, 0.3, and 0.3 (summing to 0.9).
Three pairwise disjoint events (no shared outcomes between any two of them) whose union equals the entire sample space Omega.
Three events that are each individually likely, regardless of whether they overlap.
Any three events, as long as there are exactly three of them.
assessments.explanation: A valid partition requires exactly two properties simultaneously: pairwise disjoint (no outcome belongs to more than one piece) and collectively exhaustive (every outcome belongs to at least one piece) -- option B states both correctly. Option A's probabilities summing to 0.9 rather than 1.0 is itself a red flag that the events either overlap or fail to cover Omega entirely, so it cannot be a valid partition. Option C says nothing about disjointness or exhaustiveness, both of which are required, not optional. Option D is a fabricated, meaningless requirement -- the number of pieces is irrelevant to whether a collection qualifies as a partition; disjointness and exhaustiveness are what matter.

assessments.prompt: A partition has three pieces with P(B1)=0.5, P(B2)=0.3, P(B3)=0.2, and P(A|B1)=0.05, P(A|B2)=0.20, P(A|B3)=0.60. What is P(A)?
options: 0.05 + 0.20 + 0.60 = 0.85, since you sum the conditional probabilities directly.
(0.05 + 0.20 + 0.60) / 3 = 0.2833, a simple unweighted average.
0.5(0.05) + 0.3(0.20) + 0.2(0.60) = 0.205, weighting each conditional probability by its partition piece's own probability.
max(0.05, 0.20, 0.60) = 0.60, since the largest conditional probability dominates.
assessments.explanation: The law of total probability requires weighting each P(A|Bi) by P(Bi) before summing: 0.5(0.05) + 0.3(0.20) + 0.2(0.60) = 0.025 + 0.06 + 0.12 = 0.205, exactly matching option C. Option A ignores the weights entirely, treating every branch as equally likely regardless of its actual probability. Option B computes an unweighted average, which would only be correct if all three pieces happened to have equal probability (they don't: 0.5, 0.3, 0.2). Option D confuses the overall probability with the single largest branch probability, which is not what the formula computes at all.

assessments.prompt: A Gaussian Mixture Model computes the marginal density of a point x by summing weighted component densities: P(x) = sum_k P(x | Z=k) x P(Z=k). Which concept from this module does this computation directly instantiate?
options: The multiplication principle, since it involves multiplying several numbers together.
Inclusion-exclusion, since it involves combining several probabilities into one.
The law of total probability, with the hidden mixture-component identity Z playing the role of the partition, and each component's density playing the role of a conditional probability.
Bayes' theorem, since it involves a hidden variable.
assessments.explanation: P(x) = sum_k P(x|Z=k) P(Z=k) is exactly the law of total probability's formula, with the hidden component identity Z's possible values forming the partition (each component is disjoint from the others and together they exhaust all possibilities for Z) and P(x|Z=k) playing the role of each partition piece's conditional probability. Option A misidentifies the pattern as simple multiplication, missing the summation-over-a-partition structure entirely. Option B is wrong because inclusion-exclusion specifically corrects for overlapping events, which isn't what's happening here (the components don't overlap; Z takes exactly one value). Option D jumps ahead -- Bayes' theorem does use exactly this computation internally (as its denominator), but the sum itself, in isolation, is the law of total probability, not Bayes' theorem, which is a distinct additional step covered in the next concept.

assessments.prompt: Explain the law of total probability to someone who already understands conditional probability, including why the partition requirement matters, using the multi-sub-population medical test as your worked example.
assessments.modelAnswer: The law of total probability answers the question 'what's the overall probability of some event A, when A's probability actually varies depending on which sub-group of the population you're looking at?' The trick is to split the whole sample space into a partition -- a set of pieces that are pairwise disjoint (no outcome belongs to more than one piece) and collectively exhaustive (every outcome belongs to some piece) -- and then compute P(A) as a weighted average across those pieces: P(A) = sum over each piece B_i of P(A given B_i) times P(B_i). The weighting matters enormously: a piece that's common in the population pulls the overall answer toward its own conditional probability much more than a rare piece does. The medical test example makes this concrete: split the population into young (40%, 2% disease prevalence), middle-aged (35%, 8% prevalence), and older (25%, 20% prevalence) groups, and suppose the test has 95% sensitivity and a 3% false positive rate in every group. Each group has its own probability of testing positive, computed from its own prevalence, and the overall population-wide positive rate is the weighted sum of those three group-level rates, weighted by each group's share of the population -- which comes out to roughly 8.5%, sitting between the young group's roughly 3.7% and the older group's roughly 20.9%, exactly as a weighted average should. The partition requirement isn't a technicality to skip past: if the age groups had overlapped, or left some people uncategorized, some individuals' probability of testing positive would either be double-counted or missed entirely in the sum, and the resulting 'overall positive rate' would just be a wrong number dressed up as a real one. Getting the partition right first is what makes every subsequent piece of the calculation trustworthy.

concepts.title: Bayes' Theorem and Inverse Probability
concepts.description: Bayes' theorem is the formal, always-correct way to flip a conditional probability around -- turning a known P(evidence given hypothesis) into the practically far more useful P(hypothesis given evidence) -- and it is the single piece of mathematics underneath Naive Bayes classifiers, Bayesian model updating, and the resolution of the false-positive paradox that this module's conditional-probability concept could only gesture at numerically.
learningObjectives: Derive Bayes' theorem from the definition of conditional probability applied to P(A intersect B) in both directions.
Identify the prior, likelihood, posterior, and evidence terms within a Bayes' theorem expression, and explain how the law of total probability computes the evidence term.
Work the classic false-positive-paradox medical test example end to end with real numbers and explain why the posterior can be surprisingly low even for a highly accurate test.
Explain how Bayes' theorem underlies a Naive Bayes classifier, including precisely what the conditional-independence assumption does and does not assume.
Explain Bayesian updating as the sequential, iterative application of Bayes' theorem as new evidence arrives, and connect it to updating a model's beliefs incrementally.

sections.heading: Deriving Bayes' Theorem
sections.body:
Bayes' theorem is not a new assumption about the world -- it's an algebraic identity that falls directly out of the conditional probability definition from two concepts ago, applied in both directions to the same joint event. The multiplication rule gives two equally valid ways to write P(A ∩ B): **P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B) x P(B)** and, just as validly, **P(A ∩ B) = P(B | A) x P(A)**. Since both expressions equal the same quantity, they equal each other: P(A | B) x P(B) = P(B | A) x P(A). Dividing both sides by P(B) isolates P(A | B), giving **Bayes' theorem**: **P(A | B) = P(B | A) x P(A) / P(B)**.

Relabeling with the language this theorem is usually discussed in -- A becomes a **hypothesis H**, B becomes some **observed evidence E** -- the formula reads **P(H | E) = P(E | H) x P(H) / P(E)**. This is precisely the tool that resolves the prosecutor's fallacy raised two concepts ago: it's the exact, correct procedure for converting a known P(evidence | hypothesis) into the practically far more valuable P(hypothesis | evidence), rather than assuming the two are approximately interchangeable. The denominator, P(E), is where the previous concept's law of total probability does its work: if H is one of several mutually exclusive, exhaustive hypotheses (a partition), then P(E) = Σₕ P(E | H=h) x P(H=h), summed across every possible hypothesis -- Bayes' theorem's denominator isn't a separate new formula to learn, it's the law of total probability, applied to exactly the partition formed by the competing hypotheses under consideration.

```python
def bayes_theorem(prior, likelihood, evidence):
    return likelihood * prior / evidence

# P(evidence) computed via the law of total probability across two hypotheses:
# H = has condition, H^c = doesn't have condition
prior_H = 0.001
p_E_given_H = 0.99          # sensitivity
p_E_given_not_H = 0.01       # false positive rate

evidence = p_E_given_H * prior_H + p_E_given_not_H * (1 - prior_H)
posterior_H_given_E = bayes_theorem(prior_H, p_E_given_H, evidence)
print(round(posterior_H_given_E, 4))
```

sections.heading: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior, Evidence: Naming the Pieces
sections.body:
Each term in P(H | E) = P(E | H) x P(H) / P(E) has a standard, load-bearing name. **P(H)**, the **prior**, is your belief in the hypothesis *before* seeing this piece of evidence. **P(E | H)**, the **likelihood**, is how probable the observed evidence is, assuming the hypothesis is true -- notice this is a statement about the evidence, conditioned on the hypothesis, not the other way around. **P(H | E)**, the **posterior**, is your *updated* belief in the hypothesis after incorporating the evidence -- it is literally the output of running the calculation. **P(E)**, the **evidence** (sometimes called the marginal likelihood), is the overall probability of observing E at all, regardless of which hypothesis turns out to be true, computed via the law of total probability as shown in the previous section.

This vocabulary is worth being fluent in, because it's the informal, discrete-hypothesis version of language that recurs throughout a much larger area of statistics -- full **Bayesian statistics**, where H can be a continuous parameter rather than one of a short list of discrete hypotheses, priors and posteriors become entire probability distributions rather than single numbers, and computing the evidence term often requires integration or simulation rather than a simple weighted sum. That fuller treatment (conjugate priors, credible intervals, MCMC sampling) belongs to a later module in this course -- the goal here is complete fluency with the discrete, few-hypothesis case, since every idea in the continuous case is a direct generalization of exactly the same four-term structure introduced here.

```python
def bayes_theorem(prior, likelihood, evidence):
    posterior = likelihood * prior / evidence
    return posterior

prior, likelihood, evidence = 0.30, 0.80, 0.50
posterior = bayes_theorem(prior, likelihood, evidence)
print(f"prior={prior}, likelihood={likelihood}, evidence={evidence} -> posterior={posterior}")
```

sections.heading: The False-Positive Paradox: A Worked Medical Test, Fully Resolved
sections.body:
Two concepts ago, the prosecutor's-fallacy discussion set up a scenario without the tools to finish it: a condition with prevalence 1 in 10,000, a test with 99% sensitivity (P(positive | condition) = 0.99) and a 1% false-positive rate (P(positive | no condition) = 0.01). What is P(condition | positive) -- the number that actually matters to someone who just tested positive? Bayes' theorem, with the denominator computed via the law of total probability, answers this completely.

```python
prior = 1 / 10000                     # P(condition), the base rate
p_pos_given_condition = 0.99           # sensitivity
p_pos_given_no_condition = 0.01        # false positive rate

evidence = p_pos_given_condition * prior + p_pos_given_no_condition * (1 - prior)
posterior = p_pos_given_condition * prior / evidence

print(round(evidence, 6))     # P(positive), overall
print(round(posterior, 4))    # P(condition | positive) -- surprisingly low
```

Running this gives a posterior around **0.0098**, under 1% -- despite a test that sounds highly accurate on paper. The intuition behind this seemingly paradoxical result is entirely about the base rate: because the condition is so rare (1 in 10,000), the pool of healthy people is enormous compared to the pool of people who actually have the condition, so even a small 1% false-positive rate applied to that enormous healthy pool produces far more false positives, in absolute count, than the tiny diseased pool produces true positives, even at 99% sensitivity. This is exactly why real screening programs for rare conditions always follow an initial positive with a second, different, confirmatory test -- a single positive on a rare-condition screen is nowhere near as informative as its advertised accuracy figures suggest, and this is a fully general fact about any low-base-rate detection problem, not a quirk specific to medicine. A fraud-detection model, a rare-defect inspection system, or an anomaly detector evaluated against a rare event faces the identical arithmetic: precision (the ML-flavored name for exactly this posterior) can be strikingly low even when recall and specificity both look excellent, purely because the positive class is rare.

sections.heading: From Bayes' Theorem to Naive Bayes Classifiers, and Bayesian Updating
sections.body:
A **Naive Bayes classifier** predicts the class y for a feature vector (x1, ..., xn) by choosing the class that maximizes the posterior P(y | x1, ..., xn), computed via Bayes' theorem as P(y) x P(x1, ..., xn | y) / P(x1, ..., xn). Since the denominator, P(x1, ..., xn), doesn't depend on which class y is being evaluated, it can be dropped entirely when just comparing classes against each other (it's the same normalizing constant for every candidate class, so it never changes which class wins), leaving classification as simply: pick the y that maximizes **P(y) x P(x1, ..., xn | y)** -- prior times likelihood, exactly as in the medical test, just with "class" standing in for "hypothesis" and "feature vector" standing in for "evidence."

The "naive" part is a specific, narrow simplifying assumption on the likelihood term: rather than modeling the full joint likelihood P(x1, ..., xn | y) directly (which requires enough data to estimate every feature interaction, and grows exponentially harder with more features), Naive Bayes assumes the features are **conditionally independent given the class**: P(x1, ..., xn | y) = P(x1 | y) x P(x2 | y) x ... x P(xn | y). This is precisely the chain-rule decomposition from an earlier concept, simplified by dropping every cross-feature conditional term down to just P(xi | y) -- the assumption is specifically that features don't influence each other *once you already know the class*, which is a materially different, much narrower claim than "the features are unconditionally independent of each other" or "the classes are independent of each other" (addressed directly in this concept's second misconception).

```python
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
import numpy as np

# Toy 2-feature dataset: spam (1) vs not-spam (0)
X = np.array([[3, 1], [4, 1], [1, 0], [0, 0], [5, 1], [1, 0]])
y = np.array([1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0])

model = GaussianNB()
model.fit(X, y)

new_email = np.array([[2, 1]])
print(model.predict(new_email))               # predicted class
print(model.predict_proba(new_email))          # posterior P(class | features)
```

**Bayesian updating** is simply what happens when Bayes' theorem gets applied more than once, sequentially, as evidence arrives piece by piece: today's posterior becomes tomorrow's prior. After observing evidence e1, you compute a posterior P(H | e1); when e2 arrives, that posterior slots in as the new prior, giving P(H | e1, e2) ∝ P(e2 | H) x P(H | e1) -- the same theorem, applied again, using yesterday's answer as today's starting belief. This is exactly the mechanism behind updating an A/B test's belief about which variant converts better as more visitors arrive one at a time, or incrementally refreshing an ML system's estimate of a class's prior probability as new labeled data streams in online, rather than needing to reprocess the entire historical dataset from scratch every time.

```python
# Sequential Bayesian updating over two hypotheses about a coin's fairness
hypotheses = {"fair": 0.5, "biased_toward_heads": 0.5}   # prior belief
p_heads = {"fair": 0.5, "biased_toward_heads": 0.8}

for flip_result in ["H", "H", "H", "T", "H"]:
    unnormalized = {}
    for h, prior in hypotheses.items():
        likelihood = p_heads[h] if flip_result == "H" else (1 - p_heads[h])
        unnormalized[h] = likelihood * prior
    evidence = sum(unnormalized.values())
    hypotheses = {h: v / evidence for h, v in unnormalized.items()}
    print(flip_result, hypotheses)
```

examples.title: The False-Positive Paradox, Numerically Resolved
examples.explanation: Sweeping the prior (disease prevalence) across several orders of magnitude while holding the test's sensitivity and false-positive rate fixed makes the false-positive paradox's actual cause completely transparent: at prior=0.5, the posterior is close to the test's own 99% sensitivity, but as the prior shrinks toward realistic rare-disease levels, the posterior collapses much faster, dropping under 1% by prior=0.0001. This single sweep is the clearest possible demonstration that a test's own accuracy figures (sensitivity, specificity) are almost meaningless on their own for judging what a single positive result actually implies -- the base rate is doing most of the work, and any claim like 'a positive result means X% chance of having the condition' that doesn't reference the base rate at all should be treated as suspect.

examples.title: Sequential Bayesian Updating as Evidence Arrives
examples.explanation: Each iteration of this loop is one full application of Bayes' theorem -- multiply each hypothesis's current prior by the likelihood of the observation under that hypothesis, then divide by the sum across all hypotheses (the evidence term, computed via the law of total probability over exactly this two-hypothesis partition) to renormalize back to valid probabilities that sum to 1. Feeding this loop a stream of A/B test conversion outcomes one at a time, using the previous iteration's posterior as the next iteration's prior, is exactly how a Bayesian A/B testing dashboard continuously updates its displayed 'probability variant A is better' figure as new visitors convert or don't, rather than waiting to recompute everything from a fixed, pre-collected batch of data.

examples.title: Naive Bayes' Conditional Independence Assumption, Made Explicit
examples.explanation: naive_bayes_score makes the conditional-independence assumption completely explicit and impossible to gloss over: it multiplies each individual word's probability together, one factor per word, given the class -- exactly P(x1|y) x P(x2|y) x ... x P(xn|y) rather than trying to model how 'free' and 'winner' co-occurring might interact within spam emails specifically. This is a real simplification with a real cost (words genuinely don't occur independently within a class -- 'free' and 'winner' plausibly co-occur more often in spam than the independence assumption implies), but it's precisely this simplification that makes Naive Bayes tractable to fit from a small amount of data and fast to evaluate, which is exactly the tradeoff the 'naive' in the name is honestly advertising rather than hiding.

misconceptions.description: A test that's advertised as 99% accurate means a positive result is 99% likely to mean the person actually has the condition.
misconceptions.clarification: This conflates the test's sensitivity, P(positive | has condition), with the posterior predictive value, P(has condition | positive) -- exactly the prosecutor's fallacy from two concepts ago, now fully resolvable with Bayes' theorem. As the worked example shows, for a rare condition (prevalence 1 in 10,000) even a 99%-sensitive, 99%-specific test yields a posterior around 1%, because the test's own accuracy figures say nothing about the base rate, and the base rate dominates the answer when the condition is rare. The test's advertised accuracy and the practically meaningful 'chance I actually have it, given I tested positive' are related only through the full Bayes calculation, never simply equal to each other.

misconceptions.description: Naive Bayes assumes that the different classes themselves are statistically independent of each other.
misconceptions.clarification: The assumption is conditional independence of the FEATURES given the class -- P(x1,...,xn | y) = P(x1|y) x ... x P(xn|y) -- not any claim about the relationship between different classes. Classes in a classification problem are typically mutually exclusive categories by construction (an email is spam or not spam, never both), and the 'naive' assumption says nothing about that at all; it's strictly a statement about how the features behave *within* a single class, assuming they don't influence each other once the class is already known, which is a materially narrower and more specific claim than any statement about the classes' relationship to each other.

exercises.prompt: This code tries to compute the posterior probability P(condition | positive test) using Bayes' theorem, but it returns a value greater than 1, which is impossible for a probability. Find the bug and fix it.
exercises.code:
prior = 0.001
p_pos_given_condition = 0.99
p_pos_given_no_condition = 0.02

# BUG: forgot to compute the evidence term via the law of total probability
posterior = p_pos_given_condition * prior / prior   # divides by prior instead of evidence
print(posterior)   # prints 0.99, suspiciously identical to the sensitivity -- and wrong
hints: Bayes' theorem divides by P(evidence), the overall probability of testing positive -- not by the prior itself.
P(evidence) has to be computed via the law of total probability: it's the sum of P(positive | condition) x P(condition) and P(positive | no condition) x P(no condition).
Once you compute the correct evidence term, the posterior should end up noticeably smaller than the sensitivity, not suspiciously equal to it.
exercises.solutionCode:
prior = 0.001
p_pos_given_condition = 0.99
p_pos_given_no_condition = 0.02

evidence = p_pos_given_condition * prior + p_pos_given_no_condition * (1 - prior)
posterior = p_pos_given_condition * prior / evidence   # fixed: divide by the true evidence term

print(round(posterior, 4))   # about 0.0472 -- a valid, and much smaller, probability
exercises.solutionExplanation: The bug divides by `prior` instead of by `evidence`, which algebraically cancels the prior out of the numerator entirely, leaving posterior = p_pos_given_condition exactly (0.99) regardless of what the prior even was -- a strong tell that something is wrong, since the posterior should clearly depend on how rare the condition is. The fix computes the true evidence term via the law of total probability, summing the probability of testing positive under both the condition and no-condition branches, weighted by their respective probabilities, and dividing by that correctly gives a much smaller, base-rate-aware posterior of about 4.7%, consistent with the false-positive paradox discussed throughout this concept.

assessments.prompt: In Bayes' theorem, P(H|E) = P(E|H) x P(H) / P(E), how is the denominator P(E) (the 'evidence') computed when H is one of several mutually exclusive, exhaustive hypotheses?
options: P(E) is simply assumed to equal 1, since some evidence was definitely observed.
P(E) is computed via the law of total probability: summing P(E | H=h) x P(H=h) across every possible hypothesis h in the partition.
P(E) is always equal to P(H), since they appear in the same formula.
P(E) has to be measured directly and cannot be derived from the other terms in the formula.
assessments.explanation: The evidence term is exactly the law of total probability applied to the partition formed by the competing hypotheses -- P(E) = sum over h of P(E|H=h) x P(H=h) -- which is precisely why the previous concept in this module is a direct prerequisite for this one. Option A confuses 'evidence was observed' with 'P(E) = 1', which is not implied at all; P(E) is the overall probability of that specific evidence occurring, not a certainty. Option C invents an equality with no basis in the formula. Option D is false -- the entire point of the law of total probability is that P(E) CAN be derived from the likelihoods and priors of the individual hypotheses, without needing a separate direct measurement.

assessments.prompt: A rare fraud pattern occurs in 1 out of 20,000 transactions. A fraud model flags it with 98% sensitivity and has a 3% false-positive rate on legitimate transactions. Roughly what should you expect for P(actually fraud | flagged)?
options: Roughly 98%, matching the model's sensitivity directly.
Roughly 3%, matching the false-positive rate directly.

Roughly 0.2%, since with fraud this rare, the enormous legitimate-transaction population's false positives vastly outnumber the tiny fraud population's true positives, even at a low 3% false-positive rate.
Exactly 50%, since a flagged transaction is either fraud or not, with no other information available.
assessments.explanation: This is the false-positive paradox transplanted into fraud detection: with prior = 1/20000, evidence = 0.98 x (1/20000) + 0.03 x (19999/20000) ~= 0.03005, and posterior = 0.98 x (1/20000) / 0.03005 ~= 0.00163, roughly 0.16-0.2% -- strikingly low despite seemingly strong sensitivity and specificity, exactly because fraud is so rare relative to the legitimate transaction volume. Option A repeats the exact conflation the false-positive paradox warns against. Option B confuses an input rate with the actual posterior output. Option D ignores all the given probabilities entirely and asserts an unjustified 50/50 split.

assessments.prompt: What does the conditional-independence assumption in a Naive Bayes classifier actually assume?
options: That the different classes being predicted are statistically independent of one another.
That the features are unconditionally independent of each other across the whole dataset, ignoring class labels entirely.
That the features are conditionally independent of each other GIVEN the class label -- P(x1,...,xn | y) factors into the product of each P(xi | y).
That the prior probabilities of every class must be equal.
assessments.explanation: The 'naive' assumption is specifically about the likelihood term, factoring P(x1,...,xn | y) into P(x1|y) x P(x2|y) x ... x P(xn|y) -- features don't influence each other once the class is already known, which is what makes the classifier tractable to fit and fast to evaluate. Option A misattributes the assumption to a relationship between classes, which the assumption says nothing about. Option B describes a much stronger and different claim (unconditional independence, ignoring class entirely), which is not what Naive Bayes assumes -- features can be strongly correlated overall while still being conditionally independent given the class. Option D is a fabricated requirement; class priors P(y) are estimated from data (e.g. class frequencies) and are not required to be equal at all.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a colleague how Bayes' theorem works, using the disease-test false-positive paradox as your worked example, and then explain how the same idea powers a Naive Bayes classifier.
assessments.modelAnswer: Bayes' theorem is a way to correctly flip a conditional probability around: if you know P(evidence given hypothesis), it tells you exactly how to compute the practically far more useful P(hypothesis given evidence), which is P(evidence|hypothesis) times P(hypothesis), divided by P(evidence) overall. The formula comes straight from the definition of conditional probability, written two ways for the same joint event and set equal to each other -- it isn't a new assumption, just algebra. The classic illustration is a rare disease test: suppose the disease affects 1 in 10,000 people, and the test is 99% sensitive (correctly flags 99% of true cases) with a 1% false-positive rate. It's tempting to read '99% sensitive test, positive result' as '99% chance I have the disease,' but that's confusing P(positive|disease) with the very different P(disease|positive) -- exactly the prosecutor's fallacy. Running Bayes' theorem properly, with the denominator (P(positive) overall) computed via the law of total probability across both the diseased and healthy populations, gives a posterior of roughly 1%, not 99% -- because the disease is so rare that the enormous healthy population's 1% false-positive rate produces far more false positives in raw numbers than the tiny diseased population produces true positives. Naive Bayes classifiers use exactly this same structure to predict a class y from a feature vector: compute P(y) times P(features|y) for every candidate class (dropping the shared denominator, since it's the same for every class and doesn't affect which one wins), and predict whichever class scores highest. The 'naive' part is a simplifying assumption on the likelihood term -- that features are conditionally independent given the class, so P(features|y) can be computed as the product of each individual feature's probability given y, rather than needing to model every feature interaction directly. It's the same prior-times-likelihood machinery as the disease test, just with 'which class' standing in for 'which hypothesis' and a feature vector standing in for the observed evidence.
